lesson.content: In Iceland, a combination of yellow roadside delineator posts, treeless terrain, and dark lava or moss-covered volcanic ground is a useful regional cue, though no single feature is decisive.
The Faroe Islands often combine steep basalt sea cliffs, intensely green treeless slopes, compact villages, and occasional grass-roofed buildings; the full cluster is stronger than any cue alone.
Lesotho is supported by high, dry mountain terrain together with round stone or plaster rondavel homes and patchwork cultivation on exposed slopes; similar houses elsewhere require caution.

Botswana rural scenes often show very flat semi-arid land, pale sandy shoulders, sparse thorn scrub, and long livestock fencing beside broad roads; this combination can separate it from wetter neighbors.

A solid yellow line marking the outer road shoulder is a notable South African road cue, especially when paired with left-side traffic, dry grassland, and long paved highways; the line alone is not conclusive.
Ghana can be suggested by humid roadside vegetation, reddish soil, English-language shop signs, and brightly painted commercial facades; these broad West African cues need to occur together.
Kenyan road scenes may combine left-side traffic, yellow rear license plates, highland tea fields or acacia savanna, and English or Swahili signage; landscape context helps distinguish the cue.
Uganda is supported by left-side traffic, vivid red dirt shoulders, dense equatorial greenery, and many motorcycle taxis around English-language businesses; each cue is shared with nearby countries.

Rwanda's cultivated landscape is often densely settled across steep green hills, with terraced small fields and tile-roofed homes; the concentration of farming on rolling hills is the transferable cue.
Senegal can be suggested by flat sandy Sahel terrain, French-language signs, sparse baobab or acacia vegetation, and colorful fishing pirogues near the coast; inland and coastal contexts differ.

Guatemalan highlands often combine steep volcanic terrain, concrete utility poles, cinder-block buildings, rooftop water tanks, and brightly woven local textiles; urban lowlands may lack this cluster.

Central Mexican dry regions may show agave or cactus, dusty high plateaus, concrete buildings, Spanish signage, and colorful colonial centers; vegetation plus built form is more useful than Spanish alone.

Ecuador can be supported by very high Andean valleys, concrete homes climbing green slopes, intensive small fields, and equatorial vegetation changing rapidly with elevation; coastal Ecuador looks different.

Peru's coastal desert can place dense settlements or irrigated fields directly beneath barren brown mountains, while Andean towns add brick construction and dramatic elevation; the barren mountain contrast is useful.

Bolivia's Altiplano is suggested by treeless high-elevation plains, intense clear light, unfinished red-brick buildings, and distant snowcapped Andes; lower tropical Bolivia does not share the full pattern.
Argentina's Pampas often present extremely flat open farmland, long straight roads, windbreak rows, and European-influenced small towns; Patagonia and the Andes require different evidence.

Uruguay is supported by gently rolling grassland, frequent cattle pasture, concrete utility poles, tidy low-rise towns, and broad quiet roads; it is generally greener and less vast than the Argentine Pampas.

Brazilian rural and suburban scenes can combine Portuguese text, deep red soil, orange tile roofs, concrete utility poles, and lush vegetation; Portuguese is the strongest discriminator within the Americas.
Japan is supported by left-side traffic, dense overhead wiring, narrow roads with open concrete drainage channels, vertical Japanese writing, and carefully marked utility infrastructure.
South Korea is strongly indicated by Hangul writing together with dense apartment towers, mountainous urban backdrops, green directional signs, and highly engineered roads.
Taiwan can be suggested by traditional Chinese characters, very high scooter density, tropical mountains close to dense towns, striped roadside poles, and arcaded shopfronts.

Thailand is supported by left-side traffic, distinctive Thai script, ornate spirit houses or temple roofs, tropical vegetation, and frequent concrete power poles; neighboring countries share several cues.
Malaysia often combines left-side traffic, Malay-language signs, black-and-white painted curbs, oil palms, humid greenery, and well-maintained multilane roads.
Indonesia is supported by left-side traffic, dense motorbike use, red clay roof tiles, frequent mosques, tropical volcanic terrain, and narrow busy village roads.
The Philippines can be suggested by English or Tagalog commercial signs, jeepneys, dense concrete roadside development, overhead wires, and tropical vegetation; traffic patterns vary by road.

Australian rural roads often combine left-side traffic, eucalyptus woodland, white reflector posts, broad dry shoulders, and long distances between settlements; regional vegetation still varies greatly.
New Zealand is supported by left-side traffic, lush temperate pasture, tree ferns, rugged nearby hills, and distinctive one-lane bridge warnings; drier eastern areas need additional context.
Turkey can be suggested by Turkish Latin-script place names, frequent mosque minarets, red-and-white chevron signs, dry rolling Anatolian terrain, and red tile roofs.
Greece is supported by Greek script together with olive groves, pale rocky hills, whitewashed masonry, red tile roofs, and bright dry Mediterranean light.
Albania can be suggested by steep Balkan mountains, unfinished concrete or brick homes, many roadside fuel stations, Albanian-language signs, and occasional red flags with a black eagle.
